blocks.text: 11.1.3 A Generator for 10,000-Project Portfolios

Performance work needs data at the size you will run, and GridCap's planners will not hand over next year's 10,000 real projects to a test suite. So the course generates them: `generate("large")` in the course's `gridcap` package makes a fictional portfolio of 10,000 projects over 10 years. A generated portfolio is only useful if it is the same portfolio every time someone asks for it, and if every portfolio it can make is one the model can use. This lesson takes GridCap's generator apart for those two properties: reproducible from a seed, and checked by a test of its invariants at many seeds, not one.
The Model
The generated portfolio feeds the timing model of lessons 6.4.1 and 6.4.2, which this lesson builds once per seed to check that it is feasible.

**Sets.** $`P`$ the projects; $`Y`$ the plan's years; $`T_i \subseteq Y`$ the start years project $`i`$ may use; $`M \subseteq P`$ the must-do projects; $`\mathcal{G}`$ the alternative groups; $`C \subseteq P`$ the child projects, with parent $`p(c)`$ and lag $`L_c`$ years.
**Parameters.** $`\text{npv}_{i,t}`$ ($k); $`c_{i,k}`$, what project $`i`$ spends in its $`k`$-th year of work ($k); $`B_y`$, the budget of year $`y`$ ($k).
**Variables.** $`x_{i,t} \in \{0, 1\}`$ for every $`i \in P`$ and $`t \in T_i`$.
**Objective.**
\max \; \sum_{i \in P} \sum_{t \in T_i} \text{npv}_{i,t}\, x_{i,t}
**Constraints.**

\begin{aligned}
\sum_{t \in T_i} x_{i,t} &\le 1 && \forall i \in P \setminus M && \text{(once}_i) \\
\sum_{t \in T_i} x_{i,t} &= 1 && \forall i \in M && \text{(must}_i) \\
\sum_{i \in g} \sum_{t \in T_i} x_{i,t} &\le 1 && \forall g \in \mathcal{G} && \text{(alt}_g) \\
\sum_{u \in T_c,\, u \le t} x_{c,u} &\le \sum_{s \in T_{p(c)},\, s \le t - L_c} x_{p(c),s} && \forall c \in C,\ t \in T_c && \text{(after}_{c,t}) \\
\sum_{i \in P} \sum_{t \in T_i,\, t \le y} c_{i,\,y-t}\, x_{i,t} &\le B_y && \forall y \in Y && \text{(budget}_y)
\end{aligned}
The Same Seed Gives the Same Portfolio, in This Process and in a Fresh One

A **seed** is the number a pseudo-random generator starts from: the same seed gives the same sequence of "random" numbers, so the same seed gives the same portfolio. GridCap's generator is built so that this holds byte for byte, on any machine, by three choices its docstring states:

items: **One stream, one method.** It draws every random number from one `random.Random`, seeded from the seed and the size, and calls only its `random()` method. Python's documentation guarantees that `random()` keeps producing the same sequence for the same seed across Python versions; it makes no such promise for the helpers built on top (`randint`, `choice`, `shuffle`), whose algorithms may change. The generator builds its own `between` and `pick` on `random()` instead.
**Its own integer arithmetic.** Money is rounded to integers by the generator's own code, so no library's rounding can change a cost.

**No numpy random numbers.** numpy promises the same stream for its `Generator` methods only on the same build of numpy on the same machine; a feature release may change them. That is fine for a simulation and wrong for a dataset whose hash is pinned.

blocks.text: `Portfolio.content_hash()` is the SHA-256 of the portfolio's canonical JSON (sorted keys, no spaces), so two portfolios with equal hashes are equal field for field. `gridcap`'s own tests pin the hash of every size at the default seed. `reproducible.py` checks the large one, then generates it again in two fresh Python interpreters, each with a different `PYTHONHASHSEED`, the variable that salts Python's hashing of strings (so a `set` of project ids iterates in a different order):

seed 2027: 10,000 projects, hash 092cac4f6f56f699..., pinned: True
same seed, generated again here:      True
fresh interpreter, PYTHONHASHSEED=1: True
fresh interpreter, PYTHONHASHSEED=2: True
seed 2028: hash 1c17c7e11340be98..., projects with the same id and cost profile: 25
seed 2029: hash 236a5e6e1ae0aa79..., projects with the same id and cost profile: 26

The same seed gives the same 10,000 projects in this process and in processes that hash strings differently: nothing in the generator depends on the order of a `set` or a `dict` built from hashed keys. Another seed gives another portfolio; the 25 and 26 projects that match by id and cost profile are coincidences among 10,000 draws. The hash is what a run manifest records to say which portfolio a plan was made from (lesson 10.2.4).
Generating 10,000 projects is not where a run's time goes. One run of the program on the author's machine; yours will differ:

One Shared Stream Ties Every Draw to Every Draw Before It

A single stream has a cost that shows up the first time the generator changes. Every draw takes the next number from the stream, so adding one draw anywhere shifts every number after it, and every project generated after that point changes. `streams.py` shows it on a toy generator of (kind, cost, earliest start) triples, written two ways. Version 2 adds one draw, a crew size, for distribution projects only. One way draws everything from one shared stream; the other gives each project a stream of its own, seeded from the portfolio's seed and the project's position:

def stream_per_project(n: int, seed: int, version: int = 1) -> list[tuple]:
    out = []
    for i in range(n):
        draw = random.Random(seed * 1_000_000 + i)   # project i's own stream: below a million projects, no two share one
        kind = KINDS[min(int(draw.random() * 3), 2)]
        cost = 100 + int(draw.random() * 900)
        start = 2027 + int(draw.random() * 5)
        if version == 2 and kind == "distribution":
            draw.random()
        out.append((kind, cost, start))
    return out
Each project prints as its kind's first letter, its cost and its earliest start (`d162/2027` is a distribution project costing 162 that may start in 2027):

items: **With one shared stream, project 4 (the first distribution project) took the new draw, and every project after it changed**: different kinds, costs and starts, though nothing about them was meant to change. Every test and every lesson output that used them would change too.
**With a stream per project, nothing that existed changed.** The new draw comes last in each project's own stream, so it moves no other number.

**Both are prefix-stable** here: the first 8 projects of a 10,000-project portfolio are the 8-project portfolio, because each project's draws happen in one place, in order. A generator that drew all kinds first, then all costs, would lose that: the cost of project 1 would come after 10,000 kinds in one portfolio and after 8 in the other.

**Per-project seeds must not collide.** `seed * 1_000_000 + i` gives every (seed, project) pair its own number while there are fewer than a million projects. The tempting `seed + i` would give project 1 of seed 7 the stream of project 0 of seed 8, so two "different" portfolios would share almost every project, shifted by one.

blocks.text: GridCap uses one shared stream, and accepts the cost knowingly: its tests pin each size's hash, so any change to the generator fails them, and the change then has to be made on purpose, with every lesson's output regenerated in the same commit (a comment above the pinned hashes in GridCap's generator tests says so). A generator that will keep growing fields is better served by a stream per item.
<!-- practice 1 -->
Invariants State What Every Portfolio Must Satisfy, and a Test Checks Them at Many Seeds

A reproducible generator can still make a portfolio the model cannot use. An **invariant** is a rule every portfolio must satisfy whatever the seed: something a builder, a test or a lesson relies on without checking. GridCap's are the ones its generator was written to guarantee, and the ones the timing model needs:

rows: project ids are unique
variable and row names are made from them, and names must be distinct
every project's asset exists
asset-risk models (section 7) join projects to assets
each window lies inside the horizon, with the work ending by the last year
no cost lands in a year with no budget row
an NPV for every allowed start
every $`x_{i,t}`$ has an objective coefficient
a child's parent exists and can start at least the lag before the child's latest start
otherwise every $`\text{after}_{c,t}`$ forces the child to 0
alternatives come in pairs
the $`\text{alt}_g`$ rows describe repair or replace
must-dos fit the yearly budget, started as early as they can
otherwise $`\text{must}_i`$ and $`\text{budget}_y`$ conflict
must-dos fit the regional caps the same way
models with regional caps were infeasible before this held

blocks.text: `invariants.py` writes each one as a check that returns a readable line per violation, so a good portfolio gives an empty list. Two of them:

out += [f"must-dos fit the yearly budget: {y} needs {s:,} of {p.budget[y]:,}"
            for y, s in year_spend.items() if s > p.budget[y]]

The rules are necessary, but the property that matters most is the one they are for: the model has a feasible plan. That can be checked directly, without a solver. The plan "every must-do at its earliest start, nothing else" should satisfy every row, so build the model (with lesson 11.1.2's matrix builder, which takes a tenth of a second) and multiply. With the matrix as three arrays, the value of every row for a plan $`x`$ is $`Ax`$, and `np.bincount` sums each row's terms in one call:

m = proto.linear_constraint_matrix
    rows, col, coef = np.array(m.row_ids), np.array(m.column_ids), np.array(m.coefficients)
    activity = np.bincount(rows, weights=coef * x[col], minlength=len(proto.linear_constraints.ids))
    lb, ub = np.array(proto.linear_constraints.lower_bounds), np.array(proto.linear_constraints.upper_bounds)
    return bool(np.all((lb - 1e-9 <= activity) & (activity <= ub + 1e-9)))
The program checks GridCap large at ten seeds, then plants a violation, a must-do made to cost one whole year's budget more, to show that the checks can fail:

GridCap large at 10 seeds, 8 rules: 0 violations; the must-do plan fits the model at 10 of 10 seeds
must-do projects per seed: 861 to 938

planted: P00041 made to cost one whole 2035 budget more
   must-dos fit the yearly budget: 2035 needs 1,069,530 of 918,450
   must-dos fit the regional caps: ('Valley', 2035) needs 949,220 of 418,690
   the must-do plan fits the model: False

Why ten seeds, when `gridcap`'s own tests already check these rules? Because they check them at the default seed only, and on tiny, small and medium: the large portfolio and every other seed were never checked. An invariant is a claim about *every* seed. A test at one seed checks one portfolio; a test at many seeds (the module's tests use three for large, and the program ten) is what makes "the generator never does this" believable. A check that has never failed proves little either, which is why the program plants a violation and watches both the rule and the feasibility check catch it. The two answer different questions: the plant shows that a check can fail, not that other seeds pass it, and only the checks at other seeds show that.
<!-- practice 2 -->
Count What the Generator Puts Into the Model
The generator's knobs decide the model's size, family by family. `scale.py` counts both sides for every size, using lesson 11.1.2's entry tables:

size    projects  must  child groups  starts   once  alt  after budget  nonzeros  budget nz
tiny           8     1      1      1      13      8    1      1      3        34         16
small         40     4      2      2      80     40    2      2      5       210        115
medium       400    39     18     18     887    400   18     41     10     2,550      1,426
large     10,000   871    419    575  21,843 10,000  575    882     10    63,048     35,404
Here `once` counts the once and must rows together (one per project), `starts` the variables, and `budget nz` the nonzeros in the budget rows alone. What the table says about scale:

items: **Variables grow with projects times window length**: 2.0 starts per project on small, about 2.2 on medium and large, so 10,000 projects make 21,843 binaries.
**Most rows are one per project.** The once/must rows are 10,000 of large's 11,467; the after rows grow with children times their windows (882 rows for 419 children).

**The budget rows are few and dense.** Ten rows hold 35,404 of the 63,048 nonzeros, more than half, because every start variable pays into every year its project works. Each one ties thousands of projects together, where a once row ties a project's two or three starts.

blocks.text: A generator for performance work should be checked for this too: a portfolio ten times larger whose structure is different (no children, no must-dos, all one-year projects) would measure a different model, and the speed-ups of lesson 11.1.2 would not carry over.
Summary

items: **The same seed gives the same portfolio, in this process and in a fresh one.** GridCap draws only `random()` from one seeded stream, does its own integer arithmetic, and pins each size's content hash.
**One shared stream ties every draw to every draw before it.** A new draw changes every later item; a stream per item, seeded so no two collide, changes none.

**Invariants state what every portfolio must satisfy, and a test checks them at many seeds.** Eight rules, plus a feasible plan checked as $`Ax`$ within the row bounds, hold at ten seeds of GridCap large; a planted overspend breaks both.
**Count what the generator puts into the model.** GridCap large is 21,843 binaries and 11,467 rows, and its 10 budget rows hold more than half of the 63,048 nonzeros.

blocks.text: **Further reading:** [MathOpt `model.proto` (OR-Tools source, v9.15)](https://github.com/google/or-tools/blob/v9.15/ortools/math_opt/model.proto) (the matrix as row ids, column ids and coefficients, which `witness_fits` multiplies); [Python `random`, Notes on reproducibility](https://docs.python.org/3/library/random.html#notes-on-reproducibility) (only `random()` is guaranteed to repeat across versions for a given seed); [numpy random, Compatibility policy](https://numpy.org/doc/stable/reference/random/compatibility.html) (`Generator` streams repeat only on the same build, machine and environment).

blocks.text: Design Note: A Generator Is Code Under Test Like Any Other

It is tempting to treat generated data as a fixture: produced once, trusted forever. But the generator is code, and its output is the input of every lesson and test downstream. So it gets what other code gets: a pinned output for the cases everyone uses (the content hashes), properties checked over many inputs (the invariants at many seeds), and a planted failure to prove the checks can fail. When a generator change breaks a pinned hash, that is the system working: decide whether the change is wanted, then regenerate on purpose.
